title: {{NAME}} and the Smallest Sidekick
moral: The person who notices what others miss is often the one who saves the day.
character_anchor: Bright children's book cartoon illustration, bold outlines, vivid flat colours. {{NAME}}, a young boy with brown hair and blue eyes, wearing a deep violet suit with silver gauntlets, a short silver cape, and silver boots — same child, same face, same exact outfit in every image.

pages.content:
{{NAME}} had been a junior superhero for three months and still hadn't solved a single crime on his own.

He'd helped with four. He'd contributed to seven. He'd mostly been useful at carrying things.

The problem: he couldn't fly, his strength was regular human strength, and his one actual power, being very observant, was hard to use in an emergency when things were already on fire.

Then Mote arrived.

pages.content:
Mote was a fairy, about the size of his thumb, with wings that made her invisible at speed and eyes that could see four times further than any human.

She had applied to every major superhero guild in the city. Nobody had taken her seriously.

"They see small," she said, landing on his shoulder. "You see patterns. I see details. Together we'd see everything."

"Why me?" asked {{NAME}}.

"Because you're the only one who looked at me when I knocked on their doors," she said simply.

pages.content:
Their first real mission: a building evacuation where the exits had been blocked by smoke.

Mote flew through the smoke to map every person's location, feeding {{NAME}} exact positions through his earpiece. He directed firefighters from outside with pinpoint accuracy, telling them which windows, which rooms, which floors, faster than any scanner could.

Every person was out in eleven minutes. The previous record for that building was thirty.

The fire chief looked at {{NAME}} afterward. "How did you know where everyone was?"

"Good information," said {{NAME}}.

pages.content:
After the mission, Mote sat on the rooftop wall and {{NAME}} sat beside her, both of them looking at the city.

"Eleven minutes," she said.

"Eleven minutes," he agreed.

"The guild director called me small today," she said.

"The guild director has never evacuated a building in eleven minutes," said {{NAME}}.

Mote looked at him for a moment, then made a sound that was her version of a laugh: like a tiny bell struck once.

"Same time tomorrow?" she asked.

"Every day," said {{NAME}}.

pages.content:
At home, getting ready for bed, {{NAME}} looked in the mirror at his ordinary-sized self in his violet suit.

Observation. Pattern recognition. A partner who could go where he couldn't.

He hung his cape up carefully.

On his windowsill, Mote had left a feather no bigger than a comma: one of hers, shimmering, catching the lamplight in a way that seemed like several colours at once.

He put it next to his silver gauntlets and went to sleep.

Outside, barely audible, wings moved through the night air, quick and certain and invisible.
